content: 1. Potentially Inconsistent Evidence Identified in Six Topics: The use of progesterone-only contraceptives (POCs) among breastfeeding women. The use of combined hormonal contraceptives (CHCs) among breastfeeding women. The use of CHCs in women with superficial venous disorders. The use of CHCs by different age groups. Hormonal contraceptive use among women undergoing antiretroviral therapy. The use of emergency contraceptive pills (ECPs) in women with obesity, which is a newly added condition in ECP recommendations. 2. Interim Guidance Issued by WHO Since the Fourth Edition of the Medical Eligibility Criteria (MEC): Updated guidance in 2010 on the use of CHCs during the postpartum period. Reaffirmed guidance in 2012 on hormonal contraceptive use among women at high risk of HIV acquisition and women living with HIV. 3. New Contraceptive Methods Reviewed: Sino-implant (II). Progesterone-releasing vaginal ring (PVR). Ulipristal acetate (UPA) for emergency contraception. 4. Recommendations Reviewed for Clarity by the Guideline Development Group (GDG): The use of intrauterine devices (IUDs) among women at increased risk of sexually transmitted infections (STIs), with no new evidence identified since the 2008 systematic review. The use of CHCs among women with known dyslipidemias. 5. Reaffirmation of Existing Recommendations: Approximately 2,000 recommendations from the MEC fourth edition were reaffirmed by the GDG in March 2014. Evidence was continuously monitored using the Continuous Identification of Research Evidence (CIRE) system. 6. Systematic Review Process: Systematic reviews were guided by PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome) questions to focus on studies involving populations with specific conditions or characteristics using a contraceptive method compared to those not using the method. These reviews assessed safety risks and critical outcomes. Evidence was gathered from PubMed and Cochrane databases for studies published up to January 15, 2014. Grey literature and conference abstracts were excluded. 7. GRADE Evidence Profiles: GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) evidence profiles were prepared to assess the quality of evidence and the range of effect estimates for each clinical outcome. These profiles informed the GDG’s deliberations. 8. GDG Meetings and Decision-Making: WHO convened GDG meetings in March and September 2014 to review evidence on priority topics and revise recommendations as needed. Declarations of interest were reviewed, and two members with academic conflicts of interest were excluded from deliberations on specific topics. 9. Contraceptive Use and Risk Assessment: The GDG considered the quality of safety evidence, potential harms, and benefits of preventing unintended pregnancies. Decision-making involved trade-offs among contraceptive methods, considering individual circumstances and preferences. 10. Dissemination and Evaluation of the Fifth Edition of MEC: The recommendations were released globally on June 1, 2015, during a live Facebook chat. WHO collaborated with regional offices and professional organizations to conduct regional events and international conference sessions to disseminate the guidance. An evaluation survey was planned to assess the dissemination and implementation of the guidance into national policies. 11. Specific Recommendations for CHC Use by Age Group: Women from menarche to under 40 years of age can use CHCs without restriction (MEC Category 1). Women aged 40 years and older can generally use CHCs (MEC Category 2), with consideration of cardiovascular risks that increase with age. 12. Evidence on CHC Use and Bone Health: Evidence on whether CHC use affects fracture risk is inconsistent. Some studies suggest CHC use may decrease bone mineral density (BMD) in adolescents, particularly with very-low-dose formulations (<30 µg ethinyl estradiol). However, CHC use has little to no effect on BMD in premenopausal women and may preserve bone mass in perimenopausal women. 13. Conclusion: The GDG reaffirmed the majority of existing recommendations while revising or adding new ones based on evidence.
